option: AWS ECS Fargate: one ECS service with a single task (desiredCount=1, minimumHealthyPercent=0, maximumPercent=100), arm64 image in ECR, task role, SSM Parameter Store / Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, dashboard reached by SSM port forwarding to the task's 127.0.0.1 listener. This is HLD §8.2 Option A (service/docs/ServiceHighLevelDesign.md lines 434-452).
bestCase:
THE CASE FOR FARGATE

1. The workload already fits Fargate. It is a single-active process with no inbound ports (HLD §3 LongPollingTransport; §8.2 "zero inbound security group rules"). It needs no load balancer, no service discovery and no autoscaling. Its durable state is DynamoDB plus SSM and nothing else (LLD §8.1). Runtime state is in memory by design, and a restart is made safe by startup quarantine, which is also by design (LLD §8.1 row 1; MasterSpec story 24). Nothing local has to survive a task replacement, so Fargate's disposable task model costs the design nothing. Losing an in-memory timer is the outcome the safety model already chose: the booking is preserved.

2. Single-active is enforced twice, and Fargate makes the first guard declarative. With minimumHealthyPercent=0 and maximumPercent=100, ECS stops the old task before it starts the new one. The DynamoDB INSTANCE_LEASE (LLD §8.5, lines 1026-1030) is the second guard. Under this setting the "replacement task waits ~30 s for the lease" penalty (HLD §8.2) is mostly hidden: Fargate provisioning (ENI attach, image pull, Node start) usually takes 30-90 s, so the old lease has normally expired by the time the new task asks for it. Releasing the lease explicitly on SIGTERM removes the wait for planned stops.

3. No operating system to own. This is the strongest argument in a regulated Australian enterprise. A RHEL 9 EC2 instance brings the full SOE burden: CIS hardening, monthly patch windows through SSM Patch Manager, the EDR/vulnerability/log-forwarder agents the bank mandates, AMI pipeline upkeep, and audit evidence for every one of them. All of that is for a ~20 MB Node process (MasterSpec line 108; LLD §7.2 memory estimate ~12 MB). Under Fargate, AWS patches the host and kernel. The team patches only the Node runtime and npm dependencies inside one image, and that is the part they would have to patch on EC2 anyway.

4. The artifact is immutable and rollback is one call. The image is built once, scanned (ECR enhanced scanning / Inspector) and promoted by digest. A task-definition revision pins the image digest, CPU/memory and secrets references. Rollback means redeploying the previous revision, and the ECS deployment circuit breaker does it automatically when the new task never becomes healthy. RHEL+systemd has no equivalent to "the exact bytes that ran last week" without building an AMI or artifact pipeline.

5. Security posture is easy to explain to a board:
- No inbound path at all.
- No SSH and no bastion.
- The root filesystem is read-only, and the process runs as a non-root user.
- The task role is scoped to three DynamoDB tables, with no UpdateItem or DeleteItem on audit (HLD §8.3).
- Secrets are injected from SSM SecureString / Secrets Manager by ARN, never baked into the image.
- Admin access is an IAM-authorised, CloudTrail-logged SSM session. IAM can restrict it to port forwarding only (ssm:SessionDocumentAccessCheck plus allowing only AWS-StartPortForwardingSession), so an operator who can reach the dashboard still cannot get a shell.

6. Cost is trivial. 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB arm64 runs 730 h/month for about AUD 25-30 (see cost field).

7. Recovery happens without a human. A crashed task is replaced automatically, in any AZ the service's subnets cover. Restart safety is already designed in (quarantine, lease, store-load-before-gate in LLD §8.5), so automatic replacement needs no extra correctness work.

8. On "I don't like containers": Fargate is the least-container container option. There is no cluster, node, orchestrator or Kubernetes to run. The container is used only as a packaging format, and it is the same Node process the systemd unit would run. The team writes a ~25-line Dockerfile and never manages Docker hosts.
weaknesses:
REAL WEAKNESSES (honest critic)

1. Restarts are slower, and AWS can force them. Every task replacement is a new ENI, a new IP and a new holder identity, typically 30-90 s cold, not "instant" as HLD §8.2 line 441 claims (fix that wording before the board sees it).
- AWS retires Fargate tasks for platform patching. The account setting fargateTaskRetirementWaitPeriod is 0, 7 (default) or 14 days, and AWS may override it for critical security fixes.
- Every restart, planned or not, quarantines every in-progress meeting fleet-wide until it ends. That is safe, but no ghost bookings are released for up to the length of the longest current meeting, so a mid-business-day retirement costs real value.
- MasterSpec story 23 (line 58) promises a sub-2 s restart that re-acquires the lease immediately on a VM. Fargate cannot meet that. The spec already concedes the ~30 s ECS case, but the board should hear that a Fargate restart is about 1-2 minutes.

2. A process crash means task replacement, not an in-place restart. systemd Restart=always respawns in about 1 s with the same holder ID (LLD §8.5 holder-ID rule). ECS replaces the whole task, and an un-graceful death leaves the lease to expire (~30 s). Mitigation: keep the container health check shallow (event loop alive, not Webex reachability), or a Webex or long-poll outage turns into a crash loop of quarantining restarts. The LLD already handles connectivity in-process (§7.2 onConnectivityChange).

3. Dashboard access is clunky. The task ID and container runtime ID change on every restart, so the SSM target (ecs:<cluster>_<taskId>_<runtimeId>) has to be looked up each time, which needs a helper script. ECS Exec must be enabled on the service. That bind-mounts the SSM agent and by default also allows an interactive shell, so it must be locked down with IAM (port-forward document only) and session logging. Interim shared-password auth remains (HLD §7.4), and port forwarding adds per-user IAM identity in front of it, which is a plus. Verify ECS Exec port forwarding against a distroless or minimal image in Sprint 2. Community guides confirm forwarding to 127.0.0.1 in Fargate tasks on platform 1.4.0+ with a recent SSM agent; I did not confirm it against official AWS docs.

4. Hidden network costs and dependencies. A private-subnet Fargate task needs either NAT or central egress for Webex 443, plus interface endpoints for ECR (api, dkr), CloudWatch Logs, SSM, ssmmessages and Secrets Manager/KMS (and S3 gateway for image layers). Dedicated endpoints in 2 AZs cost about AUD 200/month, roughly 8x the compute. If Suncorp's landing zone provides shared endpoints and egress over TGW, this disappears. EC2 needs most of the same endpoints anyway (ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages, logs), so the Fargate-specific delta is only ECR.

5. SMTP allow-listing. outlook.suncorp.com.au relay rules keyed to a source IP will not work, because the task IP changes on every launch. Allow a dedicated small subnet CIDR (two /28s) instead. EC2 in an ASG has the same issue on replacement.

6. Enterprise fit. Suncorp's security standards may mandate a runtime EDR agent. GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring supports Fargate through an AWS-managed sidecar, but third-party EDR on Fargate (e.g. Falcon) needs image patching or a sidecar. Check whether the platform team supports ECS at all; a "VM-only" standard would make this option moot. The team takes on a Dockerfile, ECR, image scanning and digest promotion, which is new skill for someone who dislikes containers.

7. Long-poll through egress. A NAT gateway's 350 s idle timeout, or a shorter corporate proxy timeout, can drop long-poll connections. The SDK retries every 5 s (LLD §9). This is identical on EC2, so it does not favour either option, but connectivity alarms should cover it.

8. Single-region DR is manual. Mutual exclusion through DynamoDB global tables is not safe: global-table conditional writes do not give cross-region mutual exclusion, so the lease cannot span regions. A DR region must be a pilot light at desiredCount=0, with a human cutover.

9. Doc conflicts to flag:
- HLD §8.2 describes Option A as "Min=1, Max=1". ECS services use desiredCount; there is no ASG.
- HLD §8.2 states multi-AZ only for Option B. Option A must also list two private subnets in different AZs.
- MasterSpec story 23 vs the Fargate restart time (above).
howToImplement:
CONCRETE DESIGN (ap-southeast-2, Terraform, Sprint 2 per Sprint1Spec "Deferred" items 1 and 3)

BUILD ARTIFACT
- Multi-stage Dockerfile: build `tsc` on node:22 (LTS, pinned by digest), then copy `dist/` and production node_modules only into a minimal runtime. Options are gcr distroless nodejs22-debian12, AL2023-minimal plus Node, or Chainguard; pick whatever Suncorp's registry policy allows.
- Image settings: USER non-root, no shell needed, ENTRYPOINT `node dist/main.js`, platform linux/arm64.
- CI (existing pipeline, e.g. GitHub Actions/Bamboo with an OIDC role):
  - npm ci
  - run the unit tests and the macro parity suite (`node codec-native/test_BookingAutoCancellation.js`)
  - docker buildx
  - push to ECR. Repositories are IMMUTABLE tags, scan-on-push / Inspector enhanced, with a lifecycle policy keeping the last 20 images.
  - Optional: sign with AWS Signer/Notation.
- Releases are identified by image digest. The task definition references the digest, never `latest`.

TASK DEFINITION
- requiresCompatibilities FARGATE, runtimePlatform ARM64/LINUX, networkMode awsvpc.
- cpu 512, memory 1024. 256/512 is enough for 12-20 MB of actors, but leaves no headroom for GC and the SDK.
- readonlyRootFilesystem true, with a tmpfs-like writable volume only if needed.
- stopTimeout 60.
- initProcessEnabled true, so the init process forwards signals.
- secrets[] reference SSM SecureString / Secrets Manager ARNs: WEBEX_CLIENT_ID/SECRET/refresh token, ADMIN_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD. ECS injects them at start, so no secret appears in the image or in plain env in Terraform state.
- Environment holds only non-secrets: table names, AUTOCANCEL_KILL_SWITCH parameter name, LEASE_HOLDER_ID derived at runtime from the ECS_CONTAINER_METADATA_URI_V4 task ARN.
- logConfiguration awslogs, mode non-blocking, max-buffer-size 25m, so a CloudWatch hiccup can never stall the event loop.
- Health check: `node dist/healthcheck.js`, which hits 127.0.0.1:<adminPort>/healthz and returns 200 if the event loop is responsive. It must NOT depend on Webex, SMTP or DynamoDB reachability. Settings: interval 30 s, retries 3, startPeriod 120 s.

TASK ROLE (least privilege)
- dynamodb Get/Put/Update/Query/ConditionCheck on the rooms and settings tables.
- PutItem and Query only on the audit table.
- ssm:GetParameter on the kill-switch parameter (re-read every 30 s, LLD §8.5).
- ssmmessages:* for ECS Exec.
- The execution role separately has ECR pull, logs, and secrets read.

ECS SERVICE
- desiredCount 1, launchType FARGATE with platformVersion LATEST. Never FARGATE_SPOT.
- deploymentConfiguration: minimumHealthyPercent 0, maximumPercent 100, deploymentCircuitBreaker {enable: true, rollback: true}.
- enableExecuteCommand true.
- Network: two private subnets (dedicated /28 per AZ, so the SMTP relay can allow-list the CIDR), assignPublicIp false. One security group with no ingress, and egress 443 (Webex/AWS endpoints) plus 25 to the relay IPs over TGW.
- Account setting fargateTaskRetirementWaitPeriod=14.

LEASE AND FAILOVER (extends LLD §8.5)
- Holder ID is the task ARN.
- On start: load the store, acquire the lease (conditional on attribute_not_exists OR expiry < now), and only then open the roster gate.
- Renew every 10 s with a 30 s expiry.
- On SIGTERM:
  1. close the roster gate and stop commands
  2. conditional-delete the lease where holder = me, so the next task never waits
  3. flush logs
  4. exit within 60 s
- A crash leaves the lease to expire within 30 s. That expiry overlaps the replacement's 30-90 s cold start, so it is rarely visible.
- A store outage longer than 30 s halts automation (fail-closed, unchanged).
- Active meetings are quarantined after every restart (unchanged).

DEPLOY, PATCH AND ROLLBACK
- Deploy: `terraform apply` (or `aws ecs update-service`) with the new task-definition revision, scheduled for a quiet window, ideally 22:00-05:00 AEST, because every restart quarantines in-progress meetings.
- Patch cadence: rebuild the base image weekly or on Inspector findings, and redeploy in the same quiet window. This patches Node/OpenSSL/npm, and it also restarts the task often enough that pending Fargate platform retirements land in our window rather than AWS's.
- An EventBridge rule on "ECS Task Retirement" AWS Health events pages the team, who force a new deployment that night.
- Rollback:
  - automatic, by the circuit breaker if the new task never passes health checks
  - manual, by update-service to the previous task-definition revision (digest), about 2 minutes
- Admin state in DynamoDB is untouched by either.

OBSERVABILITY
- Structured JSON logs in CloudWatch, with correlation IDs and no meeting subjects (MasterSpec story 18).
- Metrics through Embedded Metric Format, with no PutMetricData cost: releases_total{mode}, release_aborted_total{reason}, events_discarded_total{reason}, lease_held (0/1), longpoll_connected (0/1), seconds_since_last_event, smtp_failures_total, tripwire_tripped, kill_switch_active, webex_429_total.
- Container Insights (or the ECS service RunningTaskCount metric).
- Alarms to SNS, then on-call:
  - RunningTaskCount < 1 for 3 min
  - lease_held = 0 for 2 min
  - longpoll_connected = 0 for 5 min
  - seconds_since_last_event > 900 during business hours (the hourly full-state sync, LLD §7.2, means silence is abnormal)
  - tripwire tripped
  - SMTP failures > 0
  - ECS deployment failure / circuit-breaker rollback
  - AWS Health task-retirement event
- Log retention: 90 days, or whatever Suncorp policy requires. Audit trail of admin changes stays in DynamoDB (HLD §8.3).

DASHBOARD ACCESS PATH (fills the "AWS access path deferred" gap in HLD §7.4)
- The app binds 127.0.0.1:8080. In awsvpc mode the ECS Exec SSM agent shares the task network namespace.
- Operators run a wrapper script, `scripts/admin-tunnel.sh`:
  1. `aws ecs list-tasks` + `describe-tasks` to build target `ecs:<cluster>_<taskId>_<runtimeId>`
  2. `aws ssm start-session --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession --parameters portNumber=8080,localPortNumber=8080`
  3. browse http://localhost:8080/admin and log in with the shared password
- IAM for an `AutocancelAdmin` SSO permission set:
  - ssm:StartSession on the ECS task resource, plus the document AWS-StartPortForwardingSession
  - condition ssm:SessionDocumentAccessCheck = true
  - no ecs:ExecuteCommand for an interactive shell; that is reserved for a break-glass role
- SSM session logging to CloudWatch/S3. CloudTrail records who opened each tunnel, which gives per-person attribution the shared password lacks.
- Emergency stop without the dashboard: set the AUTOCANCEL_KILL_SWITCH SSM parameter to true; it takes effect within 30 s (LLD §8.5).

DR
- Within the region: ECS reschedules into either AZ automatically. RTO about 2 min, plus quarantine of in-flight meetings. RPO for admin state is 0 (DynamoDB is multi-AZ).
- Regional (ap-southeast-4 Melbourne, optional):
  - Terraform the same stack at desiredCount=0, with the ECR replication rule and SSM parameters replicated.
  - DynamoDB: PITR restore or a global table for roster, settings and audit, but the lease must NOT be relied on across regions.
  - Cutover is a human runbook: confirm primary desiredCount=0 or the region is down, scale DR to 1, re-activate nothing (the same Webex integration credentials work from any region).
  - RTO about 30-60 min manual. Because runtime state is intentionally not durable, nothing else needs replicating.

LOCAL AND TEST PARITY
- The same image runs on a laptop with `docker run`, but `npm run dev` stays the primary dev loop (HLD §8.1). No developer needs Docker to work on the service.

bestCase:
For this workload, EC2 with systemd is the best hosting choice. It is at least as safe as Fargate and better on four points that matter to this service. It also matches the user's stated preference against containers.

1. The single-instance lease works the way the docs intend. LLD §8.5 (lines ~1028-1030) sets the lease holder ID to "a stable host identity (the EC2 instance ID under systemd)". A process restart on the same host therefore takes the lease back straight away. MasterSpec user story 23 (line 58) asks for a restart "in under two seconds on a Linux VM". On Fargate every restart is a new task with a new identity. It must download the image, start, and then wait up to about 30 s for the old lease to expire (HLD §8.2 Option A; LLD §8.5). Deploys on EC2 also happen in place: swap the release link, then restart the service. The old and new process never run together, so the lease is a backup control rather than the only one. On ECS, avoiding overlap depends on minimumHealthyPercent=0 and maximumPercent=100 being set correctly (LLD §8.5). systemd also guarantees only one copy of the process exists on the host.

2. Safety does not depend on the hosting choice, and EC2 adds nothing that could weaken it. Any meeting in progress during a restart is quarantined until it ends (MasterSpec user story 24; LLD §3.2 and §5.9). Room runtime state is deliberately kept in memory only (LLD §8.1). So a restart can only cost missed release opportunities; it can never cause a wrong release. With no state on the server, an "always-on server" brings no data-loss risk. The disk holds only the OS, the release files and the log buffer.

3. The dashboard access path is solved almost for free. HLD §7.4 binds the dashboard to 127.0.0.1 and lists "the remote access path in AWS" as deferred. Session Manager's AWS-StartPortForwardingSession reaches the server's localhost port directly. It needs no inbound rule, no load balancer, no bastion host and no SSH key. Access is through IAM (IAM Identity Center users) and every session start is recorded in CloudTrail. That gives per-person attribution of who opened a dashboard session, which partly offsets the shared-password audit actor "admin". On Fargate the same thing is possible through ECS Exec, but the target is the task ID, which changes on every restart. It also requires the SSM agent to be enabled inside the task.

4. It fits how an enterprise like Suncorp runs servers. A RHEL 9 standard OS build, CIS hardening, SSM Patch Manager or Red Hat Satellite, Inspector and endpoint agents (CrowdStrike, Qualys) are normally existing, approved patterns. Fargate needs ECR, image scanning and a separately assessed runtime-security approach. For a Domain Architecture Board, "a hardened standard VM with no inbound access and no SSH" is usually a shorter conversation than a new container platform for one process.

5. Diagnosis is easier for a single process with a lot of timers. Heap snapshots, `node --inspect` over the same port-forwarding tunnel, journalctl, `systemctl status` restart counts and `ss` for long-poll sockets all work without exec'ing into a short-lived task.

6. Cost is low and does not grow with room count. About 800 actors use roughly 12 MB of heap (LLD §7.2), so a t4g.small (2 vCPU, 2 GiB) has plenty of headroom. Load is mostly network I/O: outbound long-polling, about 1 s xAPI calls, and a midnight burst spread over up to 15 minutes. Fargate does not save money at this size; costs are about the same.

7. Networking is identical to Option A. The service stays in private subnets with no inbound rules (HLD §8.2). DynamoDB is reached through the gateway endpoint (HLD §8.3) and SMTP over Direct Connect / Transit Gateway. Nothing about the enterprise network gets harder on EC2.
weaknesses:
1. The team owns the operating system. Monthly CVE patching, kernel reboots, standard-build drift, agent upgrades, disk and log-rotation housekeeping, and keeping Node.js on a supported LTS release (Node 20 went end-of-life in April 2026, so ship Node 22 or 24) are all the team's job. Fargate removes OS patching. HLD §8.2 overstates this, though: "zero AMI patching, instant container startup". Container base images still need monthly rebuilds for CVEs, and image download plus a new task plus the 30 s lease wait is not instant.

2. Every patch or deploy restart quarantines meetings in progress. Those bookings cannot be released for the rest of the meeting (MasterSpec user stories 23 and 24). This is on the preserve side, so it is safe. It still means releases are lost if patching or releasing happens in business hours. Restarts must be scheduled for 01:00-04:00 AEST to cover rooms from Perth to Sydney. This applies to any hosting option, but EC2 makes the OS patch cycle the team's responsibility.

3. A replacement server is slower than a process restart. A host or AZ failure goes through the EC2 status check (about 2-3 min), an ASG launch, boot, the release install and the about-30 s lease wait (new instance ID). That is a recovery time of about 5-10 min, versus about 1-2 min for a new Fargate task. A golden-image rollout is also a replacement, so it has the same lease wait. An ASG of 1 recovers automatically; it is not high availability. The same is true of Option A.

4. The ASG cannot see whether the application is healthy. With no load balancer, the ASG only knows EC2 status checks. A process that is running but stuck (for example, stuck without the lease, or with a dead long-poll) is invisible to it. This needs to be built: an internal watchdog that makes the process exit, systemd Restart=always, and CloudWatch heartbeat alarms that treat missing data as breaching.

5. There is a risk of configuration drift and one-off hand-configured servers if anyone gets a shell. The mitigation is no key pairs and no SSH. A shell is available only through a separate break-glass IAM role with session logging. Everything comes from Terraform, the image and the release tarball.

6. Logging takes more manual setup. The CloudWatch agent tails files, not journald. Either systemd writes stdout to a file that logrotate manages, or Fluent Bit is added. Fargate's awslogs driver needs no setup.

7. RHEL adds licence cost (billed per vCPU-hour since July 2024, unless Suncorp uses Red Hat Cloud Access with its own subscriptions). It also adds a dependency on the standard build. If the RHEL standard build is x86-only, use t3.small instead of Graviton t4g.

Risks that apply to both EC2 and Fargate, flagged here for the board:

(a) Two simultaneous long-poll connections on the same Workspace Integration may split or steal notifications. The behaviour is unverified, so replacements must never overlap. Use ASG instance refresh with MinHealthyPercentage=0, terminate first.

(b) AWS restricts outbound TCP 25 from EC2 to public IP addresses. outlook.suncorp.com.au must resolve to a private address routed over Transit Gateway / Direct Connect (Route 53 Resolver forwarding to corporate DNS). Otherwise request removal of the restriction, or use 587 with STARTTLS (SMTP_SECURE already exists in LLD fleet settings).

(c) Corporate egress to Webex may go through an explicit proxy with idle timeouts that cut long-polls. Proxy support in the SDK is unverified.

(d) LLD §8.5 should define fencing: stop issuing commands while renewal age is still less than lease TTL minus the worst-case command latency, so an in-flight CheckOut cannot land after another holder takes the lease. It should also release the lease on a clean SIGTERM.

(e) Whether the Webex refresh token rotates is unconfirmed. If it does, the service needs ssm:PutParameter on that one parameter. LLD §8.1 currently assumes read-only secrets.
howToImplement:
BUILD ARTIFACT

- CI (whichever pipeline Suncorp has approved) runs `npm ci`, `tsc` and the tests, then `npm ci --omit=dev`.
- It packages dist/, node_modules/ and a pinned official Node LTS binary (22.x or 24.x, linux-arm64 for t4g or x64 for t3) into `booking-autocancel-<semver>+<gitsha>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz`. Bundling Node means the release decides the runtime, not the OS.
- CI also produces SHA256SUMS, a CycloneDX SBOM and an optional KMS signature.
- Releases are uploaded to a versioned S3 artifacts bucket. Only CI can write to it. Object Lock is optional.
- Alternative: if the platform team distributes software through Satellite/Pulp, wrap the same tree in an RPM. Otherwise keep the tarball, which is simpler.

AMI

- The OS image comes from the existing golden-image pipeline or EC2 Image Builder. It contains RHEL 9 or AL2023 hardened to CIS, the SSM agent, the CloudWatch agent, Inspector support, chrony using the Amazon Time Sync Service, and the corporate CA bundle. It contains no application code.
- It also contains a `bac` system user with no login shell, plus /opt/booking-autocancel/{releases,current} and /var/log/booking-autocancel.
- The AMI is rebuilt monthly, and immediately for a critical CVE.

INSTANCE

- Launch template: t4g.small (or t3.small), 20 GiB encrypted gp3, IMDSv2 required with hop limit 1, no key pair, no public IP.
- Security group: no inbound rules. Outbound allows 443 to the Webex and AWS endpoints, or to the corporate proxy or egress range; 25 or 587 to the SMTP relay CIDR only; and DynamoDB/S3 through the gateway endpoints.
- ASG: min 1, max 1, desired 1, private subnets in 2 AZs, EC2 health checks, a capacity-rebalance setting that never overlaps instances, and a lifecycle hook so SIGTERM gets time to run.
- User data on boot reads `/bac/release/current-version` from SSM, downloads that tarball, checks it against SHA256SUMS, unpacks it under releases/, links current, and runs `systemctl enable --now booking-autocancel`. A replacement instance therefore always runs the approved release, not an old one built into the image.

systemd UNIT

`booking-autocancel.service` settings:
- User=bac
- ExecStart=/opt/booking-autocancel/current/node/bin/node /opt/booking-autocancel/current/dist/main.js
- Restart=always, RestartSec=2, StartLimitIntervalSec=0
- KillSignal=SIGTERM, TimeoutStopSec=20
- NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, ReadWritePaths=/var/log/booking-autocancel
- MemoryMax=1G, LimitNOFILE=65536
- StandardOutput=append:/var/log/booking-autocancel/app.json, plus logrotate with copytruncate (or Fluent Bit reading journald)

On SIGTERM the application:
1. closes the roster gate;
2. cancels timers, without clearing prompts (consistent with LLD §8.5);
3. releases INSTANCE_LEASE with a delete that only succeeds if it is still the holder;
4. exits.

An in-process watchdog makes the process exit if the event loop is blocked for more than about 10 s. systemd then restarts it.

DEPLOY

- An SSM Automation or Run Command document `BAC-Deploy` takes a `version` parameter. It downloads and verifies the release, then runs `main.js --preflight` to validate configuration, SSM reads and the DynamoDB connection.
- It records the previous `current` link, points `current` at the new version, and runs `systemctl restart`.
- It then waits up to 180 s for health: the lease is held, the long-poll is connected and the roster is loaded, reported through a 127.0.0.1-only /healthz endpoint.
- On failure it points `current` back to the previous release, restarts, and reports.
- On success it updates the `/bac/release/current-version` parameter. Releases are approved through Change Advisory Board (CAB) change records and scheduled for 01:00-04:00 AEST.

ROLLBACK

- Re-run BAC-Deploy with the previous version; the last 5 releases are kept on disk.
- Database configuration is not affected by a rollback, but changes to the DynamoDB schema must stay backward compatible for at least one release.

PATCHING

- Monthly: publish a new golden AMI, update the launch template through Terraform, then run an ASG instance refresh with MinHealthyPercentage=0. The old instance terminates (SIGTERM releases the lease) before the new one launches, so two long-polls never run at once.
- Urgent fixes between cycles: SSM Patch Manager applies security-only updates in place during the maintenance window. It reboots only if `needs-restarting -r` says so (kpatch on RHEL reduces reboots).
- Inspector v2 scans OS packages and the npm lockfile under /opt.
- Release Node versions are bumped through the normal release process.

SECRETS

- SSM Parameter Store SecureStrings, encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key: Webex client ID, client secret and refresh token, ADMIN_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD, and AUTOCANCEL_KILL_SWITCH (re-read every 30 s, LLD §8.5).
- The instance profile allows:
  - ssm:GetParameter* on /bac/*, and kms:Decrypt on that key;
  - DynamoDB access scoped to the three tables, with no Update or Delete on audit (LLD §8.2);
  - s3:GetObject on the artifacts prefix;
  - logs and CloudWatch metrics;
  - ssm:PutParameter on the refresh-token parameter only if the Webex refresh token turns out to rotate.
- No secret ever goes to disk or into environment files.

OBSERVABILITY

- The CloudWatch agent sends app.json to log group /bac/app (365-day retention, or whatever records policy requires) and sends memory and disk metrics.
- The application emits CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) records: lease_held, longpoll_connected, actors_active, checkout_total{policy}, release_aborted_total{reason}, warning_email_failed_total, smtp_errors_total, events_discarded_total{reason}, xapi_429_total, kill_switch_active, tripwire_tripped, and a heartbeat every 60 s.
- Alarms, sent through SNS to the on-call tool:
  - heartbeat missing for 3 min (missing data counts as breaching);
  - lease_held=0 for 2 min;
  - longpoll_connected=0 for 5 min;
  - tripwire tripped;
  - kill switch active for more than X hours;
  - CheckOut count above a threshold;
  - SMTP failures;
  - EC2 status check failed;
  - an ASG launch or terminate event (EventBridge);
  - NRestarts increasing (sent by the agent via procstat or a custom metric).
- A CloudWatch dashboard shows the above.

DASHBOARD ACCESS

The application binds to 127.0.0.1:8443. An admin with the IAM Identity Center role `BAC-DashboardAdmin` runs:

`aws ssm start-session --target <instance-id> --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession --parameters portNumber=8443,localPortNumber=8443`

They then open http://localhost:8443/admin and enter the shared password.

- The IAM policy allows ssm:StartSession only with that document, only to instances tagged app=bac, and only for portNumber 8443. A shell session needs a separate break-glass role, with session logs sent to S3 and CloudWatch.
- CloudTrail records who opened each tunnel. A small wrapper script (`bac-dashboard`) looks up the current instance ID from the ASG tag, because the ID changes after a replacement.
- Later, single sign-on (SSO) can be added in front of the dashboard without changing this access path.

LEASE AND FAILOVER

- The lease uses LLD §8.5 as written: holder = instance ID, TTL 30 s, renewed every 10 s.
- Add command fencing: stop all device commands once 30 s minus 5 s (worst-case command latency plus clock margin) has passed since the last successful renewal.
- Process crash: systemd restarts it in about 2 s and the same instance ID takes the lease back immediately. Meetings in progress are quarantined, then the configuration is re-applied and everything revalidated (LLD §5.12).
- Host or AZ loss: ASG replacement in another AZ takes about 5-10 min. The lease is free straight away if the old process released it on SIGTERM, otherwise after at most 30 s.
- While the service is down, rooms keep the last native CheckIn policy it wrote (LLD §5.6), and no service release happens. That is the preserve-side outcome.

DR

- Everything is in Terraform. DynamoDB has point-in-time recovery and deletion protection (HLD §8.3), plus optional AWS Backup copies to Melbourne (ap-southeast-4).
- Region loss: run Terraform for ap-southeast-4 (the stack parameterised by region), restore the tables from backup or point-in-time recovery, copy the SSM parameters through a pre-staged replication or runbook, and point at the same Webex integration.
- Targets: recovery time a few hours, recovery point minutes. This is acceptable because an outage only stops releases; it never causes a wrong one.
- Test the DR runbook once a year.

option: AWS serverless re-architecture: Webex webhooks to API Gateway and Lambda, per-room state in DynamoDB with conditional writes, timers in EventBridge Scheduler (Step Functions optional), and no long-lived process
bestCase:
This option removes containers and servers, which is the user's stated preference. The best honest case for it:

1. **Nothing to patch or babysit.** There is no AMI, systemd unit, ASG(1) or Fargate task to look after (HLD §8.2, lines ~434-452). Lambda, DynamoDB, Scheduler and SQS are all managed and multi-AZ by default. Availability and recovery should be as good as or better than Option B.

2. **No single-instance lease.** Today LLD §8.5 needs an INSTANCE_LEASE (30 s expiry, renewed every 10 s), deploys with minimumHealthyPercent=0, and has a 30 s blind window on failover. Here each room's state is serialised by a DynamoDB conditional write on a per-room `version`. That is the macro's generation model made durable. "Losing the lease halts the fleet" becomes a per-room conflict that resolves itself. Deploys need no global stop, because Lambda versions and aliases shift traffic per invocation.

3. **The generation semantics carry over well.**
   - LLD §5.1 already requires every async continuation to capture `bookingLifecycleId` and `releaseWorkflowId` and drop itself if they are stale.
   - EventBridge Scheduler delivers at-least-once, and a schedule can be deleted while it is firing. Both are exactly the "stale completion does nothing" case the macro and LLD already handle.
   - A timer becomes a one-time schedule carrying {roomId, lifecycleId, workflowId, kind}. When it fires, the Lambda re-reads the room item and returns if anything differs.
   - Duplicate fires and late cancellations are harmless by design.

4. **The core gets more testable.** The hexagonal core (HLD §3) would be refactored into a pure reducer: (state, event) → (state', effects[], timerRequests[]). That makes the macro's edge-case matrix (spec §16/§17) easier to replay deterministically than setTimeout-driven actors.

5. **Several service-only features fit the serverless model naturally.**
   - The kill switch is read on every invocation, not polled every 30 s (LLD §8.5).
   - The midnight health check is 800 per-room cron schedules, each in the codec's own IANA timezone, with jitter through flexible time windows. Scheduler supports timezones natively.
   - The tripwire becomes a DynamoDB atomic counter.
   - Audit stays append-only.

6. **Low running cost and elastic burst handling.** 9 am fleet-wide event bursts are absorbed without sizing a box.
weaknesses:
These weaknesses are serious for THIS workload. Taken together, I would not recommend the option for phase 1.

1. **Ingress turns from outbound-only into inbound internet.**
   - Webhook mode needs a public HTTPS URL. The cisco-ce/workspace-integrations-nodejs README says webhooks must be "https" on "a public site", while long polling "does not require a public web server".
   - The HLD made long polling the only transport and deferred WebhookTransport (HLD §3, lines ~55-58), and its network posture is "zero inbound security group rules" (HLD §8.2).
   - A public API Gateway plus WAF plus HMAC verification (`hmac_signature` secret) is a new internet-facing attack surface. A Suncorp security review will need to approve it, and it would be the first question from the Domain Architecture Board (DAB).
   - The alternative, a poller, cannot run as Lambda. The SDK's long poll starts inside `connect()`, has no stop method and retries forever (LLD §9). Lambda's 15-minute limit means chained pollers with gaps and duplicate sessions. That is a long-lived process in disguise.

2. **The SDK is built for a process.**
   - Token refresh is automatic in a process. In "clustered" mode the app must serialise the integration state, refresh tokens itself (`createAccessToken`, `tokenExpiryTime`) and share them, and the README says clustering "only makes sense" with webhooks.
   - Here that means a token item in DynamoDB or Secrets Manager with a refresh lock: a new correctness hazard.

3. **Ordering and coalescing are rebuilt by hand.**
   - Webhook deliveries can be processed concurrently by separate Lambdas. Per-room ordering needs an SQS FIFO queue with MessageGroupId=roomId between API Gateway and the worker Lambda. Even then, Webex delivery order is not guaranteed.
   - The 50 ms booking-sync coalescing (LLD §5.2) and the 250 ms to 4 s readiness recovery (LLD §5.3) cannot be done with Scheduler, which works at second or minute granularity with delivery jitter.
   - They become either in-invocation sleeps (paid Lambda time) or Step Functions Wait states (1 s minimum).
   - The per-device FIFO config-write queue (LLD §5.4) becomes the FIFO group.
   - This all works, but every one of these is a re-derivation of validated macro semantics, not a port of them.

4. **It contradicts a deliberate LLD decision.** LLD §8.1 keeps runtime state in memory because "persisting timers would resurrect stale workflows", with startup quarantine as the safety net. Serverless must persist timers and prompt ownership. Parity then rests entirely on generation checks at every fire, plus a re-derived "restart" concept:
   - A deploy no longer quarantines in-progress meetings. That is arguably better, but it differs from the macro and must be flagged as a parity change (CLAUDE.md requires flagging).
   - Rows that resurrect after a DynamoDB restore must be treated as a restart and quarantined.

5. **The final check-to-CheckOut window gets slightly wider.**
   - In process, JIT check 8 runs synchronously right before `checkOut()` (LLD §5.5).
   - Distributed, a concurrent Keep Booking can land between the claim and the command.
   - Mitigation: a conditional "release claim" write (pendingCheckOut + generation) before CheckOut, which the Keep Booking path must honour through the unconfirmed-guard rule. This is sound, but it is a new mechanism with no macro test behind it.

6. **The dashboard access path is forced early.** A 127.0.0.1-bound dashboard has no host to bind to (HLD §7.4). It needs one of:
   - a private API Gateway behind an execute-api VPC endpoint reached over Direct Connect, or
   - CloudFront plus Lambda behind corporate SSO.
   Either way the deferred SSO and remote-access decision now blocks go-live.

7. **Network and cost.**
   - VPC Lambdas need SMTP across TGW to outlook.suncorp.com.au:25 and HTTPS egress to Webex. That means a NAT gateway or the Suncorp shared egress VPC.
   - NAT is often the biggest line item, and VPC Lambdas pay ENI and cold-start cost.
   - Every command waits about 1 s on Webex cloud xAPI, and JIT validation is 6 to 10 sequential reads. Billed Lambda time is mostly waiting.

8. **Observability and the team.**
   - One room's workflow is spread across API GW, SQS, Lambda, Scheduler and DynamoDB, so you need X-Ray and correlation IDs to explain a single release decision.
   - The team's validated skill is an in-process event-loop macro. Distributed idempotency is a different discipline, which matters for a safety-critical, fail-closed system.

9. **Rework.** The LLD (§3 actor state, §5.1-5.4, §7.2 RoomRegistry, §8.5 lease), Sprint 1 tickets and the tracer bullet all assume an in-process actor. Large parts would need rewriting.

**Verdict:** the generation semantics survive, but only with SQS FIFO per room, conditional writes on every transition, a release-claim write, and sub-second timers moved into Step Functions. That is materially more mechanism than a single Node process on EC2 with systemd. The containerless need is fully met by Option B. Serverless is a credible phase-2 target only if webhooks and SSO are approved anyway.
howToImplement:
**Architecture: ingress**
- Webex Workspace Integration in webhook mode.
- Regional API Gateway HTTP API with WAF (Webex IP allow-list, rate limit).
- Ingress Lambda (Node 22, arm64):
  - verifies the HMAC signature;
  - drops anything not on the roster gate (cached roster read);
  - enqueues to SQS FIFO with MessageGroupId=deviceId and a deduplication ID from the event hash.
- If a public endpoint is refused, the fallback is an outbound poller. It cannot be Lambda (LLD §9), which breaks the serverless premise.

**Architecture: worker and state**
- Worker Lambda (SQS FIFO trigger, batch size 1 per group) runs the pure domain reducer.
- `rooms-runtime` table, one item per room holding phase, generations, booking ID and end time, prompt state, controllerIdsAtDisplay, uptime baseline, `version`, and a TTL.
- Every transition is a TransactWriteItems: a conditional update on `version`, plus an outbox row for side effects.
- Effects (xAPI commands, SMTP) run after commit. Each re-checks generation by re-reading before the call and after the call, mirroring LLD §5.1 "recheck after each await".
- CheckOut uses a release-claim conditional write (pendingCheckOut=workflowId) before the command.

**Architecture: timers**
- Countdown, warning, 60 s chime, prompt expiry and automatic CheckIn: EventBridge Scheduler one-time `at()` schedules targeting the SQS FIFO queue, so they serialise with events. The payload is {roomId, lifecycleId, workflowId, kind}, and `ActionAfterCompletion=DELETE`.
- Cancelling a timer is a best-effort DeleteSchedule. Correctness never depends on it.
- 50 ms coalescing: realised inside the FIFO consumer by collapsing queued availability events, then reading the snapshot once.
- 250 ms to 4 s recovery: a per-room Step Functions Standard execution with Wait states, which loses sub-second precision (1 s minimum, a documented deviation). An alternative is a bounded in-invocation retry loop of at most about 8 s.
- Midnight: one recurring Scheduler cron per enrolled room in the codec's timezone, with a 1 to 5 minute flexible window for jitter.
- Tier 2 sweeper and inventory sync: one 15-minute Scheduler cron to a sweeper Lambda (detect and block only).

**Fleet state and gates**
- Rooms, settings and audit tables unchanged (LLD §8.2).
- Kill switch: SSM parameter plus store item, read on every worker invocation with a 30 s in-memory cache per warm container.
- Tripwire: a DynamoDB atomic counter keyed by 5-minute bucket.
- Webex token: a Secrets Manager secret plus a DynamoDB refresh lock item (conditional write). One rotation Lambda refreshes 15 minutes before expiry.
- No instance lease is needed. Per-room `version` replaces it.

**Build and deploy**
- A TypeScript monorepo bundled with esbuild into zip artifacts (no containers), signed with AWS Signer, stored in S3 and deployed with Terraform (matching HLD §8.2).
- Lambda versions and aliases with CodeDeploy canary (10% for 10 min) and CloudWatch alarm auto-rollback.
- Rollback means repointing the alias. In-flight timers carry generation IDs, so an older code version that sees an unknown item shape must fail closed: preserve the booking.

**Patching**
- AWS patches the runtime. The team bumps the Node runtime major version yearly (Lambda deprecation schedule).
- npm dependencies through Dependabot and SCA in CI.

**Secrets**
- Secrets Manager or SSM SecureString for Webex client and refresh tokens, the webhook HMAC secret and SMTP credentials (if any).
- Lambda IAM roles are scoped per function. The audit table has no Update or Delete permission.

**Networking**
- Worker and sweeper Lambdas in private subnets.
- DynamoDB and SQS through VPC endpoints.
- Webex HTTPS through NAT or the Suncorp shared egress over TGW.
- SMTP:25 to outlook.suncorp.com.au over TGW and Direct Connect.

**Observability**
- Structured JSON logs (Powertools for Lambda) with roomId, lifecycleId, workflowId and correlationId. X-Ray tracing.
- Metrics: CHECKOUT count, ReleaseAbortedPreserved by reason, FIFO age-of-oldest-message, DLQ depth, Scheduler failed invocations, conditional-check-failure rate, webhook 4xx/5xx, token refresh failures.
- Alarms: tripwire, DLQ more than 0, queue age over 30 s (event lag is a safety signal, so lag over a threshold should auto-engage a per-room block), and a heartbeat on missing webhook traffic, since there is no long-poll connectivity callback. The heartbeat replaces LLD §7.2 `onConnectivityChange` and triggers fleet revalidation.

**Dashboard access**
- Server-rendered dashboard Lambda behind a PRIVATE API Gateway (execute-api VPC endpoint), reached only from the corporate network over Direct Connect.
- Interim shared password per HLD §7.4, preferably fronted by the corporate IdP (OIDC through an ALB with Lambda target) as soon as possible.
- 127.0.0.1 binding is not possible in this model.

**Failover and DR**
- Multi-AZ by default. There is no lease, so no 30 s blind window.
- Region loss: rooms preserve bookings (fail closed). DR is redeploying via Terraform into a second region plus PITR restore of the admin tables.
- Restored runtime rows must be discarded or treated as restart (quarantine), never resumed.
- Repointing the webhook URL in the Webex integration is a manual DR step.
monthlyCostEstimateAud:

| Item | AUD/month | Basis |

**Comparison:** Option B (EC2 t4g.small RHEL in ASG(1)) is roughly AUD 60-120 for compute, EBS, logs and DynamoDB, plus the same NAT or egress cost. Serverless is therefore not cheaper at this scale; the difference is driven by NAT and orchestration.

option: Enterprise on-prem / private-cloud VM (VMware RHEL 9, systemd-managed Node, inside the Suncorp network next to the SMTP relay). The admin store is either moved to a corporate PostgreSQL/SQL Server, or kept in DynamoDB and reached over Direct Connect through a DynamoDB interface endpoint, with IAM Roles Anywhere for credentials.
bestCase:
This workload is one long-lived, stateful process. Everything that matters lives in its heap: per-room actors, timers, generations and prompt ownership. Nothing is persisted (LLD §8.1, lines 977-984), and every restart quarantines every meeting in progress until it ends (MasterSpec §4, lines 110-115; LLD §5.9 line 809). So the best host is the one that restarts the process least and runs it in the most predictable network. A VMware VM is strong on both.

1. **Fewest forced restarts.** vSphere vMotion moves a running VM between hosts with its memory intact. Host patching and hardware maintenance therefore don't restart Node: timers, quarantine state and running countdowns survive. Fargate retires tasks for platform patching, and every retirement is a restart that quarantines the fleet's in-progress meetings. That is a safety-neutral loss of service, but it is a loss. Only guest-OS patching restarts the process, and the team schedules it (for example 02:00 AEST, when no meetings run).

2. **Email is local.** `outlook.suncorp.com.au:25` (HLD §8.2 line 450; MasterSpec item 7) is reached on the LAN with no Direct Connect or Transit Gateway path, and no AWS route tables or firewall changes to keep in sync. That matters because a warning-email failure blocks release for the rest of the lifecycle (LLD §5.8 line 793). Fewer network hops means fewer avoidable blocked releases.

3. **The dashboard access path already exists.** HLD §7.4 (lines 414-420) leaves the dashboard bound to 127.0.0.1 and defers the AWS access path. On-prem, admins are already on the corporate network: today an SSH tunnel through the PAM/jump host, later an internal reverse proxy with the corporate IdP (ADFS/Entra) for SSO. No SSM Session Manager, ALB or VPN work is needed. Of all the options, this one closes the open item most easily.

4. **It matches the user's preference without giving anything up.** There is no container runtime, registry, image scanning or task-definition layer. Node runs under systemd with `Restart=always`, the same supervisor model as HLD Option B (lines 442-444). The process is not horizontally scalable by design (a single active instance with a lease, LLD §8.5 line 1028), so containers' main benefits, bin-packing and scale-out, are unused here.

5. **A stable holder identity is natural.** LLD §8.5 (line 1029) wants a stable host identity for the lease so that a quick restart re-acquires it at once. A VM's UUID or FQDN gives exactly that. A replacement Fargate task gets a new identity and waits up to about 30 s.

6. **Outbound only.** Webex is reached by outbound HTTPS long-polling with no inbound ports (MasterSpec §2, lines 96-102). The docs already mention "Private Enterprise VMs" as a target (HLD line 58; MasterSpec user story 20). Nothing in the hexagonal design ties the service to AWS: only the `IFleetConfigStore` adapter, the secrets source and the log sink change.

7. **It fits an existing control set.** RHEL on VMware usually has an established CIS/Essential Eight hardening baseline, a patch cadence (Satellite), EDR, backup and SIEM onboarding. A Domain Architecture Board approves a "standard managed RHEL VM" faster than a new pattern.
weaknesses:
1. **It goes against the stated cloud strategy.** AWS is the target cloud, and every service doc is written AWS-first: Terraform, SSM `SecureString`, IAM roles, DynamoDB, VPC gateway endpoint, CloudWatch (HLD §8.2-8.3; MasterSpec §9 lines 147-155; LLD §8.2 line 990, §8.5 line 1026). Choosing on-prem means rewriting HLD §8, MasterSpec §9 and user stories 17/39, plus LLD §8.2/§8.5 (holder ID "EC2 instance ID"; kill switch "SSM parameter"). If Suncorp has a data-centre exit or VMware (Broadcom) cost-reduction programme, the Board will probably reject a new on-prem workload outright.

2. **The hybrid split is the worst of both worlds.** Compute on-prem with the store kept in DynamoDB puts the lease and the kill-switch SSM read on the Direct Connect path. The lease is renewed every 10 s with a 30 s expiry (LLD §8.5 line 1028). A DX or TGW blip longer than about 30 s therefore halts automation across the fleet. That fails closed, so it is safe, but it costs availability. It also needs IAM Roles Anywhere (a corporate PKI trust anchor) and a DynamoDB interface endpoint, which costs extra, unlike the free gateway endpoint the HLD assumes. If the service goes on-prem, it should go fully on-prem.

3. **A corporate database changes the store design.** DynamoDB conditional writes, PITR, deletion protection and IAM-enforced append-only audit (LLD §8.2 lines 992-996, §8.4 line 1018) have to be rebuilt as follows:
   - Row-version optimistic concurrency.
   - A lease row updated with `WHERE expires_at < now() OR holder = :me`, using database time to avoid clock skew.
   - A DB role with `INSERT`/`SELECT` only on the audit table.
   - DBA-managed backup and PITR.

   That is a new `PostgresFleetConfigStore` adapter and a migration-managed schema. It also adds a dependency on a shared DBA team and that team's change windows. The LLD's DynamoDB rules (version conditions, the lease) translate cleanly, but they must be re-specified and re-tested.

4. **Two consumers on one integration queue.** A warm standby must not long-poll Webex. If two processes long-poll the same Workspace Integration, they may split notifications between them. This also applies to the ECS deployment overlap. Today the LLD acquires the lease "before opening the roster gate" (§8.5 line 1028), but `connect({notifications:'longpolling'})` starts polling immediately and has no stop method (LLD §9 line 1066). So the lease must be acquired *before* `connect()`, and standby failover must start the process only once it holds the lease. **This is a doc gap to raise whichever host is chosen.**

5. **The corporate egress proxy.** Webex long-polling and the `xapi-a.wbx2.com` / `webexapis.com` calls go through the corporate web proxy, which may do TLS inspection and enforce idle timeouts. Long-polls can be cut, which makes `onConnectivityChange` fire repeatedly and triggers fleet re-apply storms (LLD §7.2 line 939, §5.12). The integration needs a proxy bypass or allowlist and no TLS inspection for the Webex domains. Node's built-in `fetch` (undici) does not honour `HTTPS_PROXY` unless configured (`NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` or an explicit dispatcher), so the SDK's proxy behaviour must be confirmed in the Sprint 1 spike.

6. **The team owns the OS.** Monthly RHEL patching, Node runtime updates, certificate and agent upkeep, and change requests through infrastructure teams usually mean days to weeks per change. Provisioning and DR rehearsal depend on other teams' queues, and Terraform coverage of vSphere is often weaker than AWS IaC.

7. **DR is manual or semi-manual.** VMware HA restarts a VM after a host failure, which takes minutes, and the restart quarantines in-progress meetings. A site loss needs SRM or a cold standby in a second data centre. Auto-healing across two sites is no better than an EC2 ASG(1) across two AZs, and is often worse.

8. **Secrets and the kill switch lose their AWS-native home.** The service needs a corporate vault (CyberArk or HashiCorp Vault) for the Webex client secret and refresh token, plus `ADMIN_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD`. The out-of-band kill switch (`AUTOCANCEL_KILL_SWITCH`, re-read every 30 s, LLD §8.5 line 1026) also needs a new source, such as a Vault KV or a database flag. If the Webex SDK rotates refresh tokens, the store must be writable by the service. That is unverified either way.

9. **Cost transparency.** The internal VMware chargeback (vCPU, RHEL subscription, backup, monitoring, SIEM) is usually higher, and less visible, than a `t4g.small` instance.

**Bottom line for the Board, stated plainly:** the user dislikes containers, and that preference is served just as well by HLD Option B (EC2 RHEL 9 + systemd, ASG 1/1). Option B keeps the AWS-native store, secrets and logging. On-prem wins only if one of these is true:
- the enterprise mandates on-prem;
- the SMTP path over DX/TGW is unreliable or slow to approve;
- dashboard SSO via an existing internal reverse proxy is needed early.

Otherwise it is a strong runner-up, not the best option.
howToImplement:
**Topology.** Go fully on-prem (not the hybrid split):
- **Primary:** one RHEL 9 VM, 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB, in the primary data centre's application VLAN, with VMware HA and DRS enabled.
- **Standby:** a cold-standby VM (or an SRM-replicated copy) in the secondary data centre, with the service *disabled* in systemd.
- **Store:** the corporate PostgreSQL cluster (HA pair with streaming replication to the DR site).

If the Board insists on DynamoDB, use a DynamoDB interface VPC endpoint reached over DX/TGW and IAM Roles Anywhere certificates from the corporate PKI. Accept that a DX outage longer than about 30 s halts automation. That fails closed.

**Build artifact.** CI (the existing GitLab/Azure DevOps/Jenkins) runs `npm ci`, the tests and `tsc`, then produces one of these:
- an RPM `booking-autocancel-<semver>.rpm` (preferred: it fits Satellite and Ansible); or
- a versioned tarball (`dist/` plus production `node_modules` and the lockfile), signed and published to Artifactory or Nexus.

The Node runtime is pinned to an LTS from the RHEL AppStream module (`dnf module enable nodejs:22`) or a vendored Node binary inside the RPM. A pinned version means OS patching never silently changes Node.

**Deploy and rollback.** An Ansible playbook does the following:
1. Installs the RPM into `/opt/booking-autocancel/releases/<ver>` and flips the `/opt/booking-autocancel/current` symlink.
2. Runs `systemctl restart booking-autocancel`.

Rollback flips the symlink back and restarts, or uses `dnf downgrade`. Deploys run only in a low-meeting window, because every restart quarantines in-progress meetings (MasterSpec §4). A restart on the same host re-acquires the lease immediately (stable holder ID, LLD §8.5).

**Unit file.** `booking-autocancel.service` (`Type=simple`):
- **Run identity and restarts:** `User=bookingsvc`; `Restart=always`; `RestartSec=5`.
- **Hardening:** `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, `ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/booking-autocancel`, `CapabilityBoundingSet=` (empty), `MemoryMax=1G`.
- **Configuration:** `EnvironmentFile=/etc/booking-autocancel/env` (non-secret settings only).
- **Liveness:** `WatchdogSec=60` with `sd_notify` from the event loop, so a hung loop is killed. No inbound health port.

**Patching.** Monthly RHEL patching through Satellite or Ansible, scheduled 01:00-04:00 AEST. The reboot quarantines in-progress meetings, which at night are none. VMware host patching uses vMotion, so the process is not restarted. Node LTS minor updates go through CI, not OS patching. Rebase onto a new Node major once a year.

**Secrets.** Store these in the corporate vault (HashiCorp Vault or CyberArk CCP):
- `WEBEX_CLIENT_ID`, `WEBEX_CLIENT_SECRET`, `WEBEX_REFRESH_TOKEN`
- `ADMIN_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD`
- the database credentials

The Vault agent authenticates with AppRole or a host certificate and renders the secrets to `tmpfs` (`/run/booking-autocancel/secrets`, mode 0400). Alternatively, the service reads them at startup through a `ISecretSource` adapter. If the Webex refresh token rotates, write it back to Vault, never to disk.

**Kill switch (the out-of-band source that replaces SSM).** Use a Vault KV key, or a separate `kill_switch` row in a schema the ops team can write with a break-glass account. Re-read it every 30 s with the same semantics as LLD §8.5: an unreadable value keeps its last value, and a value never read since startup counts as active. A second break-glass path is `systemctl stop` by on-call through PAM.

**Store schema (PostgreSQL).**
- `rooms(workspace_id PK, version int, ...)`, written with `UPDATE ... WHERE version = :v`; zero rows updated is a `ConflictError`.
- `settings(id PK, version, ...)`, including the `INSTANCE_LEASE` row:

  ```sql
  UPDATE settings SET holder = :me, expires_at = now() + interval '30 s'
  WHERE id = 'INSTANCE_LEASE' AND (expires_at < now() OR holder = :me)
  ```

  It is renewed every 10 s and uses DB time.
- `audit(entity_id, at, uuid, ...)`. The service role has `INSERT` and `SELECT` only; `UPDATE`/`DELETE` are revoked.
- Schema migrations use node-pg-migrate or Flyway. Backup and PITR are the DBA's (WAL archiving).
- The `JsonFileFleetConfigStore` laptop adapter is unchanged.

**Lease and failover.**
- Holder ID is the VM BIOS UUID or FQDN.
- **Change to the LLD:** acquire the lease *before* `connect()` starts the long poll, so a standby never consumes the integration's notifications.
- **Host failure:** VMware HA restarts the VM in about 2-5 minutes. Same holder ID, so the lease is re-acquired immediately and all in-progress meetings are quarantined.
- **Site loss:**
  1. On-call (runbook) or a Pacemaker/keepalived-free script starts the DR VM.
  2. The DR VM waits up to about 30 s for the old lease to expire, then acquires it, connects to Webex, and every actor starts with startup quarantine.
  3. Promotion of the PostgreSQL replica is handled by the DBA.
- **Target:** RTO about 15 minutes for site loss, about 5 minutes for host loss. RPO is 0 for admin state (synchronous replica) or seconds (async). Runtime state is never recovered, by design.

**Logging, metrics and alarms.**
- **Logs:** structured JSON to journald, forwarded by rsyslog or the Splunk Universal Forwarder (or Fluent Bit) to the enterprise SIEM, with correlation IDs and no meeting subject or body (MasterSpec user stories 17/18).
- **Metrics:** a local-only `/metrics` endpoint on 127.0.0.1, scraped by a node_exporter-style agent or pushed to the corporate monitoring stack (Prometheus, Dynatrace, or Splunk Observability).
- **Alarms (to the on-call pager):**
  - tripwire tripped
  - kill switch active
  - lease not held for more than 60 s
  - long-poll disconnected for more than 2 minutes
  - store unavailable
  - SMTP failures
  - `events_discarded_total` spike
  - process restarts
  - no heartbeat
- Synthetic check: a daily DRY_RUN canary room shows the pipeline end to end.

**Dashboard admin access path.**
- **Now (interim, per the HLD):** the dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1. Admins connect with `ssh -L 8443:127.0.0.1:8443` through the PAM/jump host. The PAM session is recorded, which also gives per-person attribution that the shared password lacks.
- **Next phase:** an nginx reverse proxy on the VM (or the corporate WAF/ADC) terminates TLS with an internal CA certificate and does OIDC against Entra ID/ADFS. It forwards the identity header to the app, which replaces the `admin` actor with the real user and adds roles (who may promote to LIVE).

**Network.**
- **Outbound to Webex:** egress firewall rules or a proxy allowlist for TCP 443 to the Webex domains (`webexapis.com`, `*.wbx2.com`), with no TLS inspection and a long idle timeout.
- **Email:** TCP 25 to the relay on the LAN.
- **Database:** TCP 5432 to the DB VIP.
- **Inbound:** none apart from SSH from the jump host.

**Rollout.** Keep Terraform/Ansible for vSphere (the `vsphere` provider) for repeatability. Document the variant as HLD §8.2 "Option C" with its own §8.3 store adapter.
monthlyCostEstimateAud:
Indicative only. Internal chargeback varies widely and must be confirmed with Suncorp infrastructure finance and the AWS Pricing Calculator for ap-southeast-2.

**Fully on-prem: about AUD 450-1,200/month.**
| Item | AUD per month |
| :--- | :--- |
| Primary RHEL VM (2 vCPU / 4 GB), including RHEL subscription, backup, EDR, monitoring and SIEM ingest, at typical internal chargeback | 200-450 |
| Cold DR VM or SRM replication | 80-250 |
| Schema on the shared corporate PostgreSQL HA cluster (chargeback) | 100-300 |
| Vault/CyberArk and SIEM licensing share | 50-200 |

**Hybrid (on-prem VM with DynamoDB kept): about AUD 350-950/month.** The same VM costs, plus:
| Item | Monthly cost |
| :--- | :--- |
| DynamoDB on-demand writes. Lease renewals every 10 s are about 260k writes, plus roster, settings and audit traffic | under AUD 5 |
| DynamoDB PITR | under AUD 2 |
| DynamoDB interface endpoint, 2 AZs (about USD 0.011/hour per AZ) | about AUD 25-35 |
| DX/TGW data | negligible |
| IAM Roles Anywhere | free |

**Not included:** engineering and on-call time for OS patching and change requests. That is the dominant real cost, roughly 1-2 person-days per month.

**For comparison:** HLD Option B (EC2 `t4g.small` in ASG(1), gp3 volume, CloudWatch logs, DynamoDB with a gateway endpoint) is about AUD 40-90/month in AWS charges.
